title: A restaurant kitchen for your data

beats.say: Would a restaurant serve diners straight from the delivery truck? Of course not. Data works the same way.

Raw data is the crates at the loading dock. Everything exactly as it arrived, muddy carrots and all. Only the kitchen staff go there. Next, the pantry. Things are washed, labelled and sorted, so duplicates and mistakes are gone.
Then the menu: ready-made dishes that analysts and dashboards can pick quickly. Last is the waiter's tray, the serving stage. Apps and AI assistants get exactly what they ask for, fast.

chip.text: Each reader gets a different shape

beats.say: Each stage has a different reader, so each one uses a different shape.

check.q: Why do we keep several stages instead of one set of tables?
opts: Each stage serves a different reader with a different need
Databases cannot hold more than one table
It makes the data smaller each time
check.why: The stages exist because engineers, analysts and apps need different shapes, freshness and trust. It is not about storage limits or size.

work: Name the main reader of each of your datasets in one line.
Find one place where people read raw data directly and ask why.

title: Raw to serving, step by step

beats.say: Why not one set of tables for everyone? Because a data engineer, an analyst and an app need very different things.
Bronze keeps events exactly as received, append only. If an order changes three times, you store three rows. Nothing is lost, so you can always replay.
Silver cleans up. It removes duplicates, fixes types, and keeps one row per customer or order. History is kept with start and end dates, called slowly changing dimensions type two.

show.title: Silver
items: Start and end dates for history

beats.say: Gold reshapes data for questions: a star schema, or one wide table with every column pre-joined. An analyst runs one scan instead of five joins.
Serving copies the answers into a fast store, like a key-value store, that replies in milliseconds to apps and models.

check.q: An order changes status three times. What does bronze store?
opts: All three changes as separate rows
Nothing until the order is final
check.why: Bronze is append only and as received, so every change is kept. Silver is where you reduce to the latest row and keep history deliberately.

work: Check whether your raw layer is append only and replayable.
List which tables hold history with start and end dates.

title: Where stage models go wrong

beats.say: Where do most pipelines go wrong? They model too early.
If you clean data on the way into bronze and the rule has a bug, the original is gone. You can't replay. So bronze stays raw, even when that feels messy.
In silver, ask what changes most. If sources change often, a Data Vault absorbs new columns without rebuilding. If business rules change, keep those rules out of silver.

show.title: Silver: what changes most?
items: Rules change: rules live in gold
Questions change: star or wide tables

beats.say: In gold, wide tables are fast but rigid. Change a definition and you rebuild billions of rows. And if two teams compute revenue in two places, the dashboards disagree.

show.title: Gold gotchas
items: Definition change means a big rebuild
Revenue defined twice means two answers

beats.say: In serving, the classic trap is skew: the model trains on batch values but reads different ones online.

check.q: Sources change columns every few weeks and you must audit lineage. Which silver model fits best?
check.why: A Data Vault separates keys, relationships and attributes, so new source columns are added without rebuilding the core, and every row traces back to its source.

work: Test replaying one day of bronze through your pipeline.
Search for metrics defined in more than one place and merge them.

title: Earn every layer

beats.say: Should every dataset pass through all four stages? Usually not.
Each stage is another copy and another job. Ten terabytes copied four times is forty terabytes to store, plus compute to keep them in sync, plus more things to break.
So earn each layer. One source and a small team? Go raw to a star schema, skip Data Vault. Many volatile sources and audit demands? Data Vault in silver pays off.
Rather than a wide table per team, define metrics once in a semantic layer, so BI and AI agents share one revenue number.
Add a serving store only when the latency target, say under fifty milliseconds, can't be met by the warehouse.

check.q: A small team has one source and only dashboard users. What is the best default?
opts: Raw, Data Vault, wide table, feature store, key-value store
Raw to a star schema with a semantic layer for metrics
Skip raw and transform on ingest
check.why: With one source and BI readers, extra layers add copies and cost with no benefit. Keep raw for replay, then a star schema and shared metrics.

work: Cost each layer: storage, compute and people time.
Remove or merge any layer whose reader you cannot name.
Set a latency target before adding a serving store.

title: Data is a kitchen, not a truck

beats.say: Why doesn't a restaurant cook straight from the delivery truck? Because data works the same way.
Raw data is the delivery. You keep every box exactly as it arrived, with a label saying who sent it and when. If a dish goes wrong, you can check the original.
Next, the prep kitchen washes, sorts and labels everything. One clean tub per ingredient. Then the chefs build menu dishes from it, made the same way every time.
Finally each customer is served differently. A waiter gets a quick order slip. A recipe book answers questions. Each format fits who is asking.

check.q: In the kitchen analogy, why keep the raw delivery boxes untouched?
opts: So you can go back and check or redo a dish if something went wrong
Because customers eat directly from the boxes
Because boxes are cheaper than tubs
check.why: Untouched raw data lets you replay and audit. If a cleaning rule was wrong, you can rebuild from the original.

work: Sketch your own pipeline as raw, cleaned, business and serving, and name what lives in each.
Ask which of your tables still holds the original data exactly as it arrived.

title: Raw, silver and gold: pick the model

beats.say: Where should a duplicate order be removed: when it arrives, or later?
Raw keeps an append-only log. Each row gets an envelope: source, ingested time, schema version and the payload. Ten million events in, ten million stored. Nothing is dropped, so you can replay.

Silver turns that into clean entities. Customers, orders, payments, typed and deduplicated, with history kept as slowly changing dimension type two. If many sources feed the same customer, Data Vault keeps them apart cleanly.

Gold is built for questions. A star schema, one fact table with dimensions around it, serves most analysis. A wide one big table speeds up the hottest dashboard. Daily aggregates store repeated sums once.

check.q: Which model fits the raw (bronze) stage best?
check.why: Raw must lose nothing and allow replay, so an append-only log with source, ingest time, schema version and payload fits. Stars and big tables are for answering questions later.

work: Check that your raw tables record source, ingest time and schema version.
List which gold tables are stars and which are one big tables, and why.

title: Four consumers, four serving models

beats.say: Same data, four consumers. Why not give them all the warehouse?

show.sub: Each consumer needs a different shape

beats.say: An app needs an answer in milliseconds. So load a key value store like Redis or DynamoDB, keyed by customer id. One key, one lookup, no scanning.
Machine learning gets a feature store. The offline side builds training sets as of each past moment. The online side serves the latest values. Same definitions both ways.
Analysts and language models get a semantic layer, where revenue and its joins are defined once. AI search gets a vector table: chunk text, embedding, metadata, source id and version.

show.title: BI, LLMs and AI search
items: Semantic layer: metrics, dimensions and joins defined once
Vector table: chunk, embedding, metadata, source id, version
Both sit on top of trusted gold data

check.q: What does a feature store's offline side do that a plain latest-value table cannot?
opts: Builds training rows using values as they were at each past moment
check.why: Point-in-time correct training sets need historical values as of each label time. A latest-value table would leak the future.

work: Name the consumer of each serving table you own and its latency need.
Check whether training and production compute each feature from the same definition.

title: Fixing data too early, defining it too soon

beats.say: What is the most expensive mistake in a lakehouse? Fixing data too early.

show.text: Fix it too early, lose it forever

beats.say: Clean or deduplicate on the way into bronze, and a bad rule destroys the evidence. You cannot replay what you never stored. Keep raw untouched, and fix in silver.

chip.text: Mistakes can no longer be replayed

beats.say: Put metric definitions in silver and every team inherits them, including the wrong ones. Silver should say what happened, not what revenue means.
Gold has its own trap: one table per dashboard. Soon finance reports revenue with refunds, and sales reports it without. Two numbers, one meeting, no trust. Define revenue once in shared gold models.

check.q: Why is deduplicating while loading bronze an anti-pattern?
opts: A wrong rule permanently loses data you could have replayed
check.why: Raw is your safety net. If you drop or merge rows before storing them, a mistaken rule cannot be corrected by replaying.

work: Audit ingestion jobs for filters or dedup steps that run before raw is stored.
Find metrics defined in more than one dashboard table and consolidate them.

title: Serving traps: leakage, guessing and orphans

beats.say: Why does a model score ninety percent in training and fail in production?

show.sub: Where did the gap come from?

beats.say: Often the features were computed differently. Training used a nightly SQL job; production used app code. Or training used data from after the prediction moment, which is leakage. A point-in-time correct feature store joins only values known at that time.
Language models have the same problem. Let one write SQL on raw tables and it guesses joins, and guesses revenue. A semantic layer limits it to approved metrics.
Vectors need care too. Without metadata and source version, you cannot filter by tenant or re-embed when a document changes.

show.title: A vector row needs more than a vector
items: Metadata: tenant, type, date for filtering
Source id: trace back to the document
Version: re-embed when the source changes

check.q: A feature uses an account balance that was updated after the label date. What is this problem called?
opts: Data leakage from missing point-in-time correctness
check.why: Using values not known at prediction time leaks the future into training. Point-in-time joins prevent it.

work: Check whether training features and online features come from one shared definition.
Make sure every vector row stores source id, version and filterable metadata.

title: Not every layer earns its keep

beats.say: Do you need every layer and every model? Usually not.

show.sub: Choose by need, not by checklist

beats.say: Data Vault pays off with many sources and constant change. With three sources, plain third normal form is cheaper, and the extra hubs and links just add joins.

show.title: Data Vault: only at *scale of sources*

beats.say: One big table is fast to query but duplicates dimensions. Change a customer region and you rewrite billions of rows. Keep it for the hottest questions only, built from the star.
Serving stores cost money and add sync lag. Add Redis, a feature store or a vector index only when the latency need is proven. Otherwise a warehouse with a semantic layer is enough.

show.title: Add serving stores when proven
items: Each store adds cost and a sync pipeline
Start with warehouse plus semantic layer
Add Redis, features or vectors on measured need

check.q: A team has three stable sources and only dashboard users. Which design is the best fit?
opts: Data Vault silver, Redis, and a vector index
Normalised silver, star schema gold, and a semantic layer
check.why: With few stable sources and BI users, 3NF plus stars and a semantic layer meets the need with the least cost. The others add stores and joins with no proven benefit.

work: For each extra store or model in your platform, write the measured need that justifies it.
Review any one big table: can it be rebuilt from the star in one job?

title: Taste it before you serve it

beats.say: Would a restaurant serve a dish without tasting it first?
A cook prepares the dish in the back kitchen. Nobody in the dining room can see it yet. That back kitchen is called staging, a private place to work.
Then a checker tastes it. Is it hot? Is it the right dish? Is the portion full? Only if it passes does the waiter carry it out.
Data works the same way. Write privately, check it, then publish. Customers never get a half cooked table.

check.q: In the restaurant analogy, what does the back kitchen stand for?
opts: A staging place where new data is built unseen
check.why: Staging is a private area where data is written and checked before anyone consumes it.

work: List which of your tables feed money or executive reports.
Ask where a failed load leaves its half-written data today.

title: Write, audit, publish in three steps

beats.say: How do you load a million rows and never show a customer a broken table?
Step one, write. The job lands today's data on a staging branch, not the live table. Readers still see yesterday's version.

Step two, audit. Run checks on the branch. Is the order id unique and never null? Does every customer key exist in the customer dimension? Is the row count near the usual two million, give or take ten percent? Is the latest event under an hour old?

show.title: Step two: audit the branch
items: Rows within 2M plus or minus 10 percent

beats.say: Step three, publish. If every check passes, merge or fast forward the branch, one cheap metadata swap. If one fails, the branch is dropped and the live table stays untouched.

check.q: An audit on the staging branch fails. What happens to the live table?
opts: It switches to the branch anyway
check.why: Publish only happens after all checks pass, so a failure leaves the live table as it was.

work: Pick one pipeline and write its five audit checks with thresholds.
Check whether your table format supports branches or an atomic swap.

title: Why passing checks can still lie

beats.say: Your checks passed, so why is the revenue dashboard still wrong?

show.sub: Gates only catch what you wrote down

beats.say: Because checks only catch what you wrote down. Row counts can look normal while half the amounts are zero. So add validity rules, like money never negative, and reconcile totals against the source system to the cent.
Referential integrity has a trap too. A late arriving dimension row makes foreign keys fail. Map those to an unknown member instead of blocking the whole load, and fix them later.
Decide severity. Block on broken keys and money. Only warn on small freshness drift. And remember the publish must be atomic, or readers see half of it.

check.q: Row counts are normal but half the amounts are zero. Which check would catch it?
opts: A not null check on keys
check.why: Reconciling totals with the source exposes missing money that count, key and freshness checks all miss.

work: Add a source reconciliation check to your most important money table.
Define which checks block a publish and which only warn.

title: Where gates pay off and where they don't

beats.say: Should every table get a full audit gate, and should the data team own all of it?

No. Gates cost compute and delay delivery. Audits scan data, so on a huge table check partitions that changed, not everything. Spend strict gates on money and executive tables, light ones on exploratory data.

Better still, shift left with data contracts. The producing team promises schema, meaning and freshness, and changes go through review. That stops breakage at the source, instead of at two in the morning downstream.
WAP needs branch support, like Iceberg or Delta. Without it, use a staging table and a swap. Choose by how costly a bad publish is.

show.title: Choosing the mechanism
items: Match rigor to cost of a bad publish

check.q: What is the main benefit of data contracts compared with downstream audits alone?
opts: They prevent breaking changes at the producer before they spread
check.why: Contracts move agreement upstream so schema changes are reviewed, while downstream audits remain a safety net.

work: Tier your tables and set gate strictness per tier.
Propose a contract with your top event producer covering schema and freshness.

title: Pantry, meal tray, menu board

beats.say: Why would anyone store the same sales numbers three different ways? Picture a restaurant kitchen.
A star schema is a pantry. Receipts sit in the middle. Small labeled shelves surround them: customers, products, cities. You can cook any dish, but you fetch from several shelves each time.

chip.text: Flexible, but you fetch from shelves

beats.say: One big table is a ready meal tray. Everything is already on one plate, so serving is instant. The catch is that it is one fixed meal.

chip.text: Fast to serve, one fixed view

beats.say: Aggregates are the menu board. Totals per city per day, counted once, so nobody recounts every receipt. Copy the board from the receipts, never type it by hand, or it drifts.

check.q: Which analogy best fits an aggregate table?
opts: A menu board of totals copied from the receipts
A ready meal tray holding every detail
check.why: An aggregate stores precomputed summaries at a coarser grain, such as city by day, derived from the base records.

work: List the three dashboards your team opens most and note which shape each one reads today.
Ask who owns each summary table and whether it is generated from the base fact.

title: Star, wide table, aggregate: the mechanics

beats.say: A dashboard wants yesterday's trips by city. Should it read fifty million rows, or three hundred?
In a star, one fact row is one trip, holding keys and numbers like fare. Keys point to small dimension tables: rider, city, date. Every question joins the fact to the dimensions it needs.

A one big table does that join once, ahead of time. Fare, city name and rider tier sit side by side in one wide row. Columnar engines read only the columns asked for, so width is cheap and the query needs no join.
An aggregate goes further. Group trips by city and day, and fifty million rows shrink to about three hundred. Dashboards that repeat the same summary all morning read that instead.

check.q: Why is a wide table cheap to scan on a columnar engine?
opts: It stores fewer rows than the fact
Only the requested columns are read, so extra columns cost little
It never needs to be rebuilt
It compresses rows into one file
check.why: Columnar storage reads just the columns a query touches, so width adds little scan cost while removing the join.

work: Write down the grain of your main fact in one sentence.
Pick one repeated dashboard query and estimate rows scanned with and without an aggregate.

title: Physical layout of a lakehouse fact

beats.say: Why can the same table take two seconds or two minutes? Often it is the physical layout, not the model.

Partition the big fact by event date. A query for yesterday then opens one folder and skips the rest. Inside it, cluster or sort by the most common filter, such as city, so matching rows sit together.

chip.text: Skip what you do not need

beats.say: Aim for files of about 128 megabytes to one gigabyte. Ten thousand tiny files mean ten thousand opens and listings, and that slows every query.
Finally, use nested types. A trip can carry an array of stops inside one row, so you avoid yet another join.

show.title: Nested types
items: An array holds many stops in one trip row

check.q: A lakehouse fact has millions of 100 KB files. What is the main problem?
opts: Per-file open and listing overhead slows queries
check.why: Small files multiply metadata and open costs. Compact into files of roughly 128 MB to 1 GB.

work: Check the median file size of your largest fact and schedule compaction if it is tiny.
Confirm the table is partitioned by event date and sorted by the top filter column.

title: Fan-out and the frozen view

beats.say: Your one big table shows revenue double what finance reports. What went wrong?
Fan-out. You joined trips to payments, and one trip has two payments. Now the trip row appears twice, and its fare is counted twice. Joining along any one-to-many path multiplies rows.
Prevent it by checking row counts after every join against the fact's grain. Aggregate the many side first, or nest it as an array.

show.title: Guard the grain
items: Assert rows out equal rows in
Or nest it as an array

beats.say: Second trap: a rider's city is corrected in the dimension. The wide table still holds the old value, so you must rebuild affected partitions. And remember, it freezes one view of the data.

check.q: After joining trips to payments, summed fares are too high. Most likely cause?
check.why: A trip with several payments repeats on each payment row, so its fare is summed more than once.

work: Add a row-count assertion after each join in your wide-table build.
Document which dimension corrections trigger a rebuild and how far back.

title: Drifting totals and as-of joins

beats.say: Two dashboards show different totals for the same city and day. Why?

show.text: Same city, same day, two totals

beats.say: Someone defined an aggregate separately from the base fact. One excludes cancelled trips, the other does not. The fix is to generate every aggregate from the fact with one shared query, never hand-maintain it.

Star schemas have their own gotcha. When a rider's tier changes, history is kept as dated versions of the dimension row. Analysts must join where the trip date falls between a version's start and end. That is an as-of join. Forget it, and old trips take today's tier.

show.title: As-of join
show.text: join dim_rider r on t.rider_id = r.rider_id and t.trip_date between r.valid_from and r.valid_to
show.note: Match the version live on the trip date

check.q: Why do analysts need an as-of join on a history-tracking dimension?
opts: To match each fact to the dimension version valid on the event date
check.why: With several versions per rider, a plain key join would match all of them or the latest, giving wrong history.

work: Replace any hand-written summary tables with ones generated from the base fact.
Provide a ready-made as-of view so analysts never write that join themselves.

title: Choosing among star, OBT and aggregates

beats.say: Should you just flatten everything into one big table and delete the star?
No. Keep the star as the flexible core. It serves many questions, and shared conformed dimensions mean every team uses the same definition of city or rider.

Then generate the wide table and aggregates from it for the hottest dashboards and text-to-SQL, where a model writing joins often gets them wrong. You pay storage and rebuild compute to save query cost and mistakes.

show.title: What you trade
items: Pay: extra storage and rebuild compute
Save: query cost and join errors
Win: simple tables for BI and text-to-SQL

beats.say: Skip the wide table when questions change daily or dimensions are corrected often. For entity history and states, use cumulative tables, and accept sequential backfills.

show.title: When not to
items: Questions change daily: stay on the star
Entity history: cumulative tables, slow sequential backfills

check.q: Best architecture for many teams plus a few very hot dashboards?
opts: Star core, with generated wide tables and aggregates for hot paths
check.why: The star keeps flexibility and shared definitions. Generated derivatives speed hot paths without letting definitions drift.

work: Identify the three hottest dashboards and build generated wide tables only for them.
Track rebuild cost per derived table so you can retire ones that no longer pay off.
Test text-to-SQL accuracy on the star versus the wide table before choosing.

title: Why a model must not peek at the future

beats.say: Imagine sitting an exam when someone slipped you the answers. You would score perfectly. Then you would fail the real one. Why does this matter for data?

show.sub: Models can cheat without anyone noticing

beats.say: A model that predicts whether a trip will be cancelled can only use what was known when the rider asked. If we attach today's rider statistics to an old trip, the model has peeked at the future.

A feature store fixes this. A feature is just a fact the model uses, like cancellations in the last thirty days. The store remembers each fact with a timestamp, so every old trip gets what was known then, not what is known now.

check.q: Why does a model trained with today's rider statistics on old trips fail in production?
opts: It used facts that were not known at request time
check.why: Using future information inflates offline scores. In production those facts do not exist yet, so performance drops.

work: Ask your ML teams what timestamp each training feature is joined on.
List features that are recomputed as of today rather than stored with a date.

title: One dictionary for every number

beats.say: Three people ask for revenue last week and get three different numbers. How can that happen?

One analyst leaves out refunds. Another counts unfinished trips. Each wrote their own formula. A semantic layer is a shared dictionary. It defines revenue once, in code, along with the ways you can slice it, such as by city.
Now dashboards, notebooks and AI assistants all ask for revenue by city, and the layer writes the same query every time. For an AI, it is choosing from a menu instead of guessing how tables join.

check.q: What is the main benefit of defining revenue in a semantic layer?
opts: Queries run faster on raw tables
Every tool gets the same definition and the same number
It removes the need for a warehouse
check.why: The layer centralises the formula, dimensions and joins, so every consumer, including AI agents, gets consistent results.

work: Pick your three most disputed metrics and write down who defines each.
Move one metric definition into a shared, version-controlled file.

title: As-of joins and the online store

beats.say: A rider has five cancellations on Monday and twelve on Friday. Which number does a Tuesday trip get for training?
Five. The feature store keeps every value with a timestamp. For each training row, an as-of join picks the latest value at or before the trip's request time. Never after.
For live traffic, an online store keeps only the newest value per rider in a key-value database. A lookup takes a few milliseconds.
Both paths come from one feature definition, so what the model learned on is what it sees in production.

check.q: A trip is requested Tuesday. Feature values exist for Monday and Friday. Which does an as-of join use?
opts: Monday, the latest value at or before the request
check.why: As-of joins take the most recent value not later than the event time, preventing future leakage.

work: Check that your feature tables store a valid-from timestamp.
Test one training set by confirming no feature timestamp is later than its event time.

title: Building a vector table for retrieval

beats.say: How does an AI assistant find the one paragraph, among a thousand runbooks, that answers your question?

show.text: One paragraph in a thousand documents

beats.say: You split each document into chunks of a few hundred words. Each chunk becomes an embedding, a list of numbers that captures its meaning. Similar meanings sit close together, so search means finding the nearest numbers.
Store beside each chunk its text and metadata: source, owner, date, access level and version. Then you can filter, such as only payments runbooks this person may see.
Add a content hash. When a document is edited, only chunks whose hash changed get re-embedded, which saves cost.

check.q: What is the content hash on a chunk used for?
opts: Detecting which chunks changed so only those are re-embedded
check.why: Comparing hashes shows what changed, so you avoid paying to re-embed unchanged chunks.

work: Add source, owner, access level, version and hash columns to your chunk table.
Measure how much embedding spend a hash check would save on one nightly refresh.

title: Why a great offline model flops live

beats.say: Your model scored ninety-five percent offline and flopped live. What do you check first?

Leakage. Typical causes are joining on when a record was processed instead of when the event happened, or using late-arriving data that was not available at request time. An as-of join on the wrong timestamp still leaks.

show.title: Leakage suspects
items: Processing time used as event time

beats.say: Next, training-serving skew. If training computes a feature in batch and serving recomputes it in app code, small differences creep in. One shared definition prevents that.
Also watch freshness. An online value that stopped updating hours ago quietly serves stale data. Set a time to live and alert on its age.

check.q: Training computes a feature in a batch job. Serving recomputes it separately in application code. What risk is this?
check.why: Two implementations drift apart, so the model sees different values live than it learned on.

work: Audit which features have two separate implementations.
Add an age alert on online store values.

title: Stale chunks, leaked chunks

beats.say: You updated a policy, but the assistant still quotes the old one. Why?
Stale chunks. If you embed the new text without deleting the old version, both stay in the index. Use the document version, and delete or filter out anything not current.
Second, access. If a restricted chunk is retrieved before permissions are checked, the model can reveal it. Filter by access level inside the search, not after.

show.title: Access control
items: Never trust the prompt to hide data

beats.say: Third, embeddings from different models are not comparable. Change the model and you must re-embed everything, so record the model name on every row.

show.sub: Store the model name per row

check.q: Where should access-level filtering happen in retrieval?
opts: After the model writes its answer
Inside the search query, before results reach the model
check.why: Filtering at query time guarantees restricted chunks never reach the model; later or prompt-based controls can fail.

work: Check that every chunk row carries version, access level and embedding model name.
Test that old document versions are removed after an update.

title: Do you really need a feature store?

beats.say: Should every team that trains a model adopt a feature store?
No. If you only score in batch, a warehouse table with a valid-from timestamp and an as-of join gives point-in-time correctness without running extra systems.
An online store earns its cost when you need millisecond lookups and share features across many models. Then you pay for streaming pipelines, a key-value store and backfills.
Rule of thumb: start with as-of joins in the warehouse, and add the online store when latency demands it.

check.q: A team only scores customers once a night. What is the sensible choice?
opts: Warehouse feature tables with as-of joins
check.why: Batch scoring needs correctness, not millisecond serving. Warehouse as-of joins give that without extra infrastructure.

work: List models needing under 100 ms feature lookups; only those justify an online store.
Estimate the running cost of streaming and backfills before buying a platform.

title: Choosing semantic layers and vector stores

beats.say: Where do you put metric logic, and where do you put vectors?
A semantic layer beats wide tables when many tools and AI agents need consistent answers. But it adds a service, and complex ad hoc analysis still needs raw SQL. Do not force everything through it.

show.title: Semantic layer
items: Win: one definition for all tools

beats.say: For vectors, a few million chunks fit in Postgres with a vector extension, beside your metadata and permissions, with simple filters and transactions. Past tens of millions, or under heavy query load, consider a dedicated vector database.
Choose by scale, filter needs and who owns operations, not by hype.

check.q: You have two million chunks, strict per-user permissions and a small team. What is a sound default?
opts: Postgres with a vector extension, keeping metadata beside the embeddings
Flat files read by the model
check.why: At this scale Postgres handles vectors well, and keeping permissions and metadata in one place simplifies filtering and operations.

work: Count chunks and peak queries per second before choosing a vector store.
Write down which metrics truly need cross-tool consistency and put only those in the layer.

title: Blank page: where do you start?

beats.say: Someone says: design the data for a taxi app. You have a blank page and forty-five minutes. Where do you even start?

show.sub: Design the data for a taxi app

beats.say: Not with boxes. Start with questions. What does the boss need to know? Revenue per city, trips per driver, late pickups. Write down five. That list is your target, like a shopping list before you enter the shop.

Next, list what happens: trips, payments, ratings. Then list who is involved: rider, driver, city. Finally say in one sentence what one row means. One row is one completed trip. That sentence is called the grain, and everything else hangs on it.
Then say your reasons out loud as you go. Interviewers score your thinking, not your drawing.

check.q: What is the grain of a fact table?
opts: The list of columns it has
One sentence saying what a single row represents
The size of the table in gigabytes
The tool used to load it
check.why: The grain says what one row means, such as one completed trip. Measures and dimensions are only valid once that is fixed.

work: Before your next design review, write down the five questions the model must answer.
Write the grain of each table as one sentence in its description.

title: Dimensions and facts around the grain

beats.say: You have the grain: one row per completed trip. What goes around it?

show.text: Grain: one row per completed trip

beats.say: Dimensions describe the who and where. Rider, driver, city, date. For each attribute that changes, pick a history rule. A driver's phone number? Overwrite it, that is type one. A driver's city? Keep every version with dates, that is type two, because Finance reports by city at trip time. Rider and driver are the same person table, used in two roles.

Now the fact table. Transaction type, one row per trip. Measures: fare, distance, tip. Those add up across anything, so they are additive. Driver rating average does not add, so store the sum and the count. Keep the trip id on the row itself, a degenerate id, with no table of its own.

check.q: Average driver rating per trip is stored. How should you keep it so it can be rolled up by city?
opts: Store the average and sum it
Store the rating sum and rating count
Store it only in the dimension
Round it to a whole number
check.why: Averages are not additive. With sum and count you can add both across any grouping and divide at the end.

work: Review one fact table and label each measure additive, semi-additive or non-additive.
List which dimension attributes truly need history before choosing SCD2.

title: Prove it, then scale it

beats.say: How do you prove a model works before the clock runs out?

Take two of your five questions and write the query. One easy: fare by city by day, a join and a group by. One needs history: revenue by the driver's city at trip time. That is an as-of join. Match each trip to the dimension row where trip time falls between valid-from and valid-to.

Then scale and evolve. Partition trips by date, say about two million rows a day. Late events? Reload the affected day. Duplicates? Dedupe on trip id. A new source or attribute? Add a column or dimension, not a rebuild. And say which layer each table lives in.

show.title: Scale and evolve
items: New attribute: add, do not rebuild
Name the layer of each table

check.q: A report needs revenue by the driver's city at the moment of the trip. What do you need?
opts: Join to the current driver row
An as-of join to an SCD2 dimension on trip time
check.why: Only versioned history lets you recover the city that was true at trip time, and the as-of join picks that version.

work: Write one as-of join on your own data and check each trip matches exactly one row.
Write down how late and duplicate events are handled for your busiest fact.

title: Why strong candidates still fail

beats.say: Why do strong candidates still fail this round?

Mistake one: skipping the grain. Mix one row per trip with one row per payment, and a join doubles revenue. Mistake two: type two on everything. A rider's email changing creates millions of useless rows. Mistake three: a sloppy as-of join. Use valid-from less than or equal to trip time, and trip time less than valid-to, or boundary trips match twice.
Also watch ratios and balances. Averages and account balances cannot be summed across time, so store the parts. And never go silent. A diagram with no spoken trade-off scores low.

check.q: A fact joins to a dimension and total revenue doubles. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The dimension has overlapping or duplicate rows for the key
check.why: Duplicate or overlapping dimension versions make one fact row match twice, inflating sums.

work: Add a test that each fact key matches exactly one dimension row.
Audit your SCD2 tables for attributes that never need history.

title: Spending 45 minutes like a budget

beats.say: Forty-five minutes, one design. How do you decide what to leave out?
Spend time like money. About five minutes clarifying, ten on grain and dimensions, ten on facts, ten proving with queries, and ten on scale. Hold the rest back for questions.

Then name the alternative. If one team just needs dashboards, a wide one big table is cheaper to query but harder to change. If many sources keep arriving, a Data Vault raw layer absorbs change, with star schemas on top for serving. A semantic layer defines revenue once.
And say when you would not model at all. Tiny data, one question, a single report? A view is enough.

check.q: Many new source systems keep arriving, and a team also needs fast dashboards. What is a sound choice?
opts: One big table loaded directly from every source
A Data Vault integration layer with star schemas for serving
check.why: A vault absorbs source change without rework, while stars give simple fast reads for dashboards.

work: Practise a mock round with a timer and the five stage budget.
For one project, write down why you chose its layers and what you would use if scale doubled.

title: Crates and prep kitchen: raw and cleaned

beats.say: Why keep a messy copy of your data and a clean copy too?
Think of a restaurant. Crates arrive from suppliers and go in the storeroom untouched, with the delivery date on each one. That is the raw layer: data exactly as received, only ever added to.
Then the prep kitchen washes, trims and weighs everything into standard portions. That is the cleaned layer: no duplicates, the same units, one clock.
If a recipe goes wrong, you go back to the crates and prep again. Throw the crates away, and you can never prove what arrived.

show.title: Why keep the crates
items: Redo the cleaning when a rule was wrong
Prove what the source really sent

check.q: A cleaning rule turns out to be wrong. What lets you fix it fully?
opts: Edit the cleaned tables by hand
Reprocess from the untouched raw layer
Ask the source to resend everything
check.why: Raw is kept exactly as received and never edited, so you can rerun cleaning with a corrected rule and rebuild the cleaned layer.

work: Check whether your pipeline overwrites or keeps the original landed files.
Ask where you would go to prove what a source sent last March.

title: Hubs, links and sticky notes: Data Vault

beats.say: How does a bank keep every fact from ten systems about one customer, and never lose any?
Picture a library card catalogue. Each person gets one index card showing only their ID number. That card is a hub: just the business key, nothing else.
A link is a string between two cards: this rider took a trip with that driver.

Details go on sticky notes pinned to a card, each stamped with a date and its source. Those are satellites. Nothing is erased; new notes are just added. A new system just means a new note, and no card changes.

check.q: A new system starts describing your riders. In a vault, what do you add?
opts: A new column on the hub
A new satellite attached to the existing hub
A new copy of every table
check.why: Satellites hold descriptive attributes per source, so a new source is a new satellite and existing tables stay untouched.

work: Sketch one business entity of yours as a hub with two satellites.
List which systems describe the same customer in your company.

title: How raw and cleaned layers work

beats.say: A source sends the same order twice and renames a column overnight. What happens to your tables?
Raw lands it append-only, in a folder per ingestion date, wrapped in an envelope with the source name and arrival time. Say five million rows a day, written once and never edited.
With Iceberg or Delta, schema evolution lets you add, rename or widen a column without rewriting old files. Time travel lets you read yesterday's version.

show.title: Table formats help raw
items: Time travel: read an older snapshot

beats.say: Cleaned then removes the double order, casts strings to dates and decimals, converts times to UTC, and maps each source's customer key to one shared key. It keeps history with type two slowly changing rows, or snapshots.

check.q: Why is schema-on-read acceptable in the raw layer?
opts: Raw only stores what arrived, and strict checks happen when cleaning
check.why: Raw's job is to capture faithfully. Enforcing types and rules is the cleaned layer's job, so source changes don't break ingestion.

work: Check raw tables are partitioned by ingestion date with source and arrival time recorded.
Write down your dedup key for each cleaned table.

title: Hubs, links, satellites in motion

beats.say: How can three kinds of table model a whole business?
A hub holds the business key, like rider id, plus a hash of it called the hash key, a load timestamp and the source. One row per key, ever.
A link stores each trip: the rider hash key, the driver hash key and the trip id.

Satellites carry the attributes. One from the app database holds name and city. Another from the ratings service holds rating. Each row has a hash diff, a fingerprint of its columns. If the fingerprint changes, insert a new row. If not, skip it.
Because keys are hashed from the business key, tables load in parallel with no lookups.

check.q: What is the job of hash_diff in a satellite?
opts: Join the satellite to the hub
Detect whether the attributes changed, so a new row is inserted only when needed
check.why: hash_diff fingerprints the descriptive columns. Comparing it to the latest row tells the loader whether anything changed.

work: Draw hub, link and satellites for one of your entities, with the hash key columns.
Decide which columns go in which satellite by source and change rate.

title: Vault gotchas interviewers probe

beats.say: Why does nobody query a data vault directly?

Even asking for a rider's city and latest rating means a hub, two satellites, and picking the newest row per key in each. Many joins. So teams build point-in-time tables and then star schemas or wide tables on top.

Next, the hash. If one loader trims spaces or uppercases keys and another does not, the same rider gets two hash keys, and your history silently splits. Null handling in hash diff causes the same trouble.

show.title: Hashing traps
items: Standardise case, trim and nulls before hashing
One hash rule for every loader
Pick a stable business key, not a source surrogate id

beats.say: Finally, load timestamp is when you received data, not when it happened. Late arrivals and satellites split too finely, or lumped too widely, make rows explode or hide change.

show.title: Time and design traps
items: load_ts is arrival time, not event time
Split satellites by source and change rate
Too many tiny satellites means more joins

check.q: Two loaders hash the same rider id, one trimmed and one not. What happens?
opts: The rider gets two hub rows and history splits
check.why: Different input strings give different hashes, so the same entity appears as two keys, silently breaking joins and history.

work: Write one shared hashing function and test it on whitespace, case and nulls.
Add point-in-time tables before exposing vault data to analysts.

title: Vault, Kimball or one big table?

beats.say: When is a data vault the wrong answer?
With two or three sources and a small team, a vault adds tables, modelling effort and a second layer you must still turn into marts. Going from cleaned straight to a Kimball star ships weeks sooner.

Choose a vault when many systems describe the same entities, sources change often, and auditors need insert-only history, as in banks and insurers. A new source then costs one satellite, not a redesign.

For lakehouse analytics, medallion layers feeding one big table is simpler and fast to query. The strong answer: Kimball for clear reporting, vault for the enterprise core, one big table for lakehouse serving, and a marts layer on top of any of them.

check.q: A startup has three sources and four analysts. Which is the best default?
opts: Full Data Vault with marts on top
Cleaned layer feeding a Kimball star or wide tables
check.why: With few sources and little audit pressure, the vault's extra layer and effort are not repaid. A dimensional model on cleaned data delivers value faster.

work: Count your sources per core entity and your audit needs before proposing a vault.
Prepare a one-minute answer comparing vault, Kimball and one big table.
